q: What makes Sandakphu–Phalut special?
a: The route combines a famous Himalayan panorama with an extended ridge walk, mountain villages and forest descents. Phalut adds a substantial walking challenge beyond a Sandakphu-only visit.

q: Can we see Everest from Sandakphu?
a: On clear days, Everest can be seen in the distant western mountain group with Lhotse and Makalu. Clouds and haze can hide the view completely.

q: What is the Sleeping Buddha?
a: It is the reclining-figure outline associated with Kangchenjunga and its neighbouring peaks. Your guide can help you identify the skyline when visibility permits.

q: Is this trek easy or moderate?
a: For this full itinerary, moderate is the more useful description. The first climb, approximately 21 km Phalut stage, long descent and consecutive walking days demand preparation.

q: Can a first-time Himalayan trekker join?
a: A well-prepared beginner may be suitable after discussing fitness and health with the organiser. Previous short hikes and back-to-back walking practice will help.

q: Do I need climbing skills or ropes?
a: The usual route is non-technical. Snow, ice or severe weather can still make sections unsafe and may require equipment changes, rerouting or cancellation.

q: Is there an age limit?
a: The organiser must set the participation policy. Suitability depends on health, fitness and supervision; do not describe this itinerary as suitable for every age without assessment.

q: How high do we go?
a: The highest planned point is Sandakphu, approximately 3,636 m. Accommodation elevations and published readings vary slightly; Phalut is around 3,600 m.

q: How far do we walk in total?
a: Budget approximately 80–85 km for the proposed complete walking route. The total will be revised after the vendor confirms trail choices and the final pickup point.

q: How long is the longest walking day?
a: Sandakphu to Phalut is approximately 21 km. Allow roughly 8–10 hours, sometimes longer, including breaks and depending on weather and group pace.

q: Why does the programme begin with Day 0?
a: Day 0 is the arrival and transfer day, including the Manebhanjang overnight stay. Days 0–6 total seven calendar days; it is not an extra day outside the package.

q: How many nights are included?
a: The revised plan contains six: Manebhanjang, Tumling, Kalpokhri, Sandakphu, Phalut and Gorkhey. The vendor must confirm and price all six.

q: Is Srikhola an overnight stop?
a: Not in this seven-day plan. We walk to the confirmed Srikhola roadhead and transfer to Siliguri on Day 6.

q: Can the long Phalut stage be split?
a: Potentially, if authorised accommodation and logistics allow. An extra ridge night changes the programme unless another stage is redesigned; it needs a separate agreement.

q: Are all route spellings the same places?
a: Common variants include Manebhanjang/Maneybhanjyang, Kalpokhri/Kalipokhri, Gorkhey/Ghorkey and Srikhola/Shrikola. Match bookings to the actual property and pickup location.

q: Which airport should I book?
a: Bagdogra Airport, code IXB. Siliguri is the regional meeting hub, but the airport is a separate pickup location that must be confirmed.

q: Which railway station is best?
a: New Jalpaiguri, code NJP, is the main long-distance rail gateway. Check the booking carefully; it is not the same station as Siliguri Junction.

q: Can I fly from Kochi?
a: Yes, search COK–IXB connecting itineraries. Prefer one protected booking and confirm that the arrival time works with the group transfer.

q: Can I fly directly from Bengaluru?
a: Non-stop BLR–IXB options may be available for your dates. Verify the actual flight before booking; route pages do not guarantee daily non-stop operation.

q: Which trains should I consider from Ernakulam?
a: Check Vivek Express and Aronai Express services to NJP. Verify the current service number, ERN or ERS boarding station, running day and seat availability in IRCTC/NTES.

q: When should I reach Siliguri?
a: Preferably the evening before Day 0. A same-day arrival is workable only if it meets the organiser’s confirmed pickup cutoff with a realistic delay buffer.

q: Can I book a flight on Day 6?
a: This is not recommended. A full morning’s walking followed by a long drive makes a reliable airport arrival difficult. Stay in Siliguri and fly the next day.

q: Is the final Siliguri hotel included?
a: Not in the proposed six-night trek plan. Ask for a separate hotel and transfer arrangement if you want BOOTpaths to coordinate it.

q: Are airport and station pickups included?
a: Only if the final quotation specifically says so. A Siliguri group pickup does not automatically include separate transfers from IXB and NJP.

q: What if my flight or train is late?
a: Contact the organiser immediately. A delayed pickup or catch-up transfer depends on road access and staffing and may cost extra; catching the group cannot be guaranteed.

q: Does the trail go along the Nepal border?
a: Yes, parts of the traditional route and some accommodation lie along or across the border. The guide must confirm the permitted route and overnight arrangements for every participant.

q: What identification should an Indian participant carry?
a: Carry original government-issued photo ID and copies. Because Nepal-side access may be involved, confirm the accepted documents for this exact itinerary; do not assume Aadhaar alone is sufficient.

q: Can foreign nationals join?
a: Only after the operator verifies nationality-specific park, border, visa, accommodation and route restrictions. A route suitable for Indian nationals cannot automatically be promised to everyone.

q: Are permits included?
a: The source offer includes permits and local taxes. Confirm which permits, nationality categories and any additional fees are covered in the revised quote.

q: Can I add Darjeeling before or after the trek?
a: Yes, as a separate travel arrangement. Allow sufficient time and clarify luggage, hotel and transfer costs; it is not part of the stated route.

q: Will we stay in tents every night?
a: No. The intended style is simple mountain accommodation. The vendor’s tent alternative requires advance confirmation of equipment, permits, facilities and suitable conditions.

q: Will I have a private room?
a: Not necessarily. Sharing and dormitory arrangements depend on the properties and group size. Request your preference early; single rooms may be unavailable.

q: Are toilets attached to the rooms?
a: Do not assume so. Shared toilets are common in basic trekking accommodation. Confirm property-specific arrangements and any accessibility concerns before booking.

q: Will there be hot showers and heating?
a: These are not guaranteed. Hot water may be limited or paid, and rooms may be unheated. Bring adequate warm layers and follow the host’s heating-safety instructions.

q: What food will be served?
a: Expect simple local meals suited to trekking. The exact menu depends on supplies and kitchens. Long walking days may require packed lunches.

q: Can vegetarian or special diets be arranged?
a: Vegetarian meals are generally practical, but all requirements need notice. Strict allergy, vegan or gluten-free needs require direct confirmation of ingredients and kitchen limitations.

q: Is drinking water provided?
a: The final package must specify treated-water provision and charges. Carry reusable bottles and ask about refills before each day; untreated streams are not a safe default.

q: Will I get mobile reception and Wi-Fi?
a: Coverage is patchy and Wi-Fi cannot be relied on. Near the border, watch for unintended roaming. Give family a realistic communication plan before leaving.

q: Can I charge my phone or camera?
a: Some properties offer limited charging, sometimes at extra cost. Bring a power bank and protect batteries from cold; do not rely on a socket every night.

q: Can I pay digitally on the trail?
a: Sometimes, but network and electricity failures can interrupt payment. Carry enough small-denomination cash for agreed extras and keep it secure.

q: Can I offload my backpack?
a: Only if porter or animal support is arranged. Confirm availability, charges, weight limits, route coverage and suitable working conditions. Carry all daytime essentials yourself.

q: What shoes should I wear?
a: Well-fitting, broken-in trekking shoes with reliable grip. Test them on descents with your trekking socks. Bring more weather-resistant footwear if winter conditions require it.

q: Do I need a sleeping bag?
a: That depends on the confirmed bedding and accommodation plan. Ask before packing or renting, especially for Phalut and winter departures.

q: Are trekking poles useful?
a: Yes, especially on the long descent and uneven ground. Practise using them beforehand and stow them safely in crowded rooms and vehicles.

q: What should I carry for menstrual care?
a: Bring the products you normally use, spare underwear, sanitiser and sealable disposal bags. Water and privacy can be limited; carry used products out for proper disposal.

q: Will we definitely see snow?
a: No. Snow depends on recent weather, season and elevation. Winter may bring bare, icy ground as well as snowfall; either can affect the route.

q: When is the park closed?
a: The usual monsoon closure is 16 June–15 September. The operator must check current park orders, temporary restrictions and the opening status for your exact dates.

q: Will we see a red panda?
a: Possibly, but sightings are rare and never guaranteed. Keep quiet, remain on the trail and follow the guide’s wildlife- distance instructions.

q: How fit should I be?
a: Prepare for repeated long walks with hills and your planned pack. Use the eight-week plan and discuss difficulty completing practice outings with the organiser.

q: Can I get altitude sickness even if I am fit?
a: Yes. Fitness is not protection against altitude illness. Follow the reporting and ascent guidance in the health section. [8]

q: What if I have headache or nausea?
a: Tell the guide immediately and do not continue ascending while symptomatic. Worsening symptoms or serious warning signs require descent and medical help.

q: Should I take Diamox preventively?
a: Discuss acetazolamide with a qualified clinician before travel. Do not use another trekker’s prescription or treat medication as a substitute for an appropriate ascent plan.

q: Can I join with a medical condition?
a: Disclose relevant conditions, allergies and regular medicines. Seek individual clinical advice and confirm that the trek’s remoteness and support arrangements are appropriate for you.

q: Is a doctor or oxygen cylinder included?
a: The vendor lists a guide’s first-aid kit only. Doctor support, oxygen, trained staffing and emergency equipment must be separately confirmed before they are advertised.

q: How does evacuation work?
a: The guide coordinates the safest available route and transport. Weather, communication and road access can delay help; there is no assumed helicopter or immediate vehicle rescue.

q: Do I need insurance?
a: Trek insurance is included in this cost. BOOTpaths gives safety the first priority and hence the insurance made compulsory.

q: What happens in severe weather?
a: The route, timings or overnight stops may change, or the trek may end early. Participant safety and legal access take priority over completing the advertised route.

q: Can I use a drone or play music?
a: Do not assume drone permission in this protected border landscape. Avoid loud music; keep the experience quiet for wildlife, residents and fellow trekkers.

q: What are the cancellation and early-exit rules?
a: See BOOTpaths’ policy covering cancellation, replacement, weather changes, missed transfers, unused services and extra costs before payment.
